value.overview: The White-throated Shrike-Tanager is a distinctive Central American tanager with a strongly hooked bill, long tail, and contrasting white throat. It inhabits humid lowland and foothill forests, where it usually forages in the middle and upper levels of vegetation. Costa Rica is an important part of its range and supports resident populations on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes. The species is often encountered alone, in pairs, or in small family groups accompanying mixed-species flocks.
value.classification: The White-throated Shrike-Tanager belongs to the tanager family Thraupidae and the genus Lanio. Several geographically distinct subspecies are recognized, including forms occurring in Costa Rica.
value.identification: This is a medium-sized, slender tanager about 20 cm long, with a relatively long tail and a conspicuously hooked black bill. Adult males are mainly black above, with a white throat, buffy or pale ochre breast, and yellow underparts; some Pacific birds have additional black on the rump and undertail. Females and immature birds are browner or rufous above, with a paler throat and yellowish underparts. The heavy bill and white throat help separate it from similar shrike-tanagers.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from eastern Honduras through Nicaragua and Costa Rica to western Panama. In Costa Rica it is a resident, locally uncommon to fairly common in humid lowlands and foothills, generally from about 100 to 900 m, with some regional variation. It occurs along the Caribbean slope and in adjacent foothills, and also on the southern Pacific slope north to the Carara area. It favors mature tropical evergreen forest, tall humid woodland, forest edges, and other dense, well-vegetated habitats, usually in rolling terrain.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered non-migratory and resident. Individuals in Costa Rica remain year-round, although they may make local movements through forest and foothill habitats in response to food availability or seasonal conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited. In Costa Rica, a cup-shaped nest has been reported on a low shrub near a stream in forest. The clutch is usually two white eggs marked with gray-brown and chocolate-colored spotting, concentrated toward the larger end. Nesting activity has been recorded around May, with recently fledged young observed in July. The nest is placed low in vegetation, making dense understory and streamside cover important during reproduction.
value.dietFeeding: Detailed dietary studies are scarce, but the species is primarily an insect-eater and takes other invertebrates. Its hooked bill is suited to seizing and handling relatively large prey. It forages actively through the middle and upper levels of humid forest, probably taking insects from foliage, twigs, and other surfaces and occasionally making short sallies. Fruit or other plant material may also be consumed opportunistically, as in many tanagers.
value.behavior: White-throated Shrike-Tanagers are usually seen singly, in pairs, or in small family groups of about three or four birds. They commonly join mixed-species flocks with other tanagers, antbirds, woodcreepers, and flycatchers. Their movements through dense foliage can be deliberate but active, and the species may be easier to detect by its calls than by prolonged views. It is generally a forest bird that uses both middle and upper vegetation layers.

conservation.populationTrend: The population is considered to be declining, largely because suitable humid forest is being lost or degraded across parts of its range. Precise population estimates and detailed long-term trend data are limited.
conservation.threats: The principal concern is the continuing loss and fragmentation of humid lowland and foothill forest caused by agricultural expansion, cattle pasture, infrastructure, logging, and other land-use changes. Degradation of forest edges and streamside vegetation may reduce nesting and foraging habitat. Because the species has a relatively restricted range, additional habitat loss in Costa Rica and neighboring countries could have a disproportionate effect.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore mature humid forest, especially lowland and foothill forests on both Caribbean and southern Pacific slopes. Maintain connected forest corridors, streamside vegetation, and large trees within protected areas and private reserves. Encourage wildlife-friendly farming and shade production near forest remnants, support monitoring of resident populations, and report observations through reputable bird-monitoring programs to improve knowledge of distribution and trends.
